title: Clean Ruby
content:
## General Code Standards
- Write clean and readable ruby code.
- Follow the Single Responsibility Principle; each method should do one thing.
- Use descriptive method names.
- Extract validation, transformation, and complex conditionals into helper methods.
- Use snake_case for methods/variables, CamelCase for classes/modules, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants.
- Rescue specific exceptions and use descriptive messages.

## Code Stylistic Requirements
- Group similar methods.
- Use early returns.
- Use guard clauses and early returns for edge cases.
- Document complex code.
- Keep methods under 20 lines and cyclomatic complexity under 7.
- Break long lines (>100 chars) with line continuations.
- Keep lines under 100 chars.
- Use single quotes for strings without interpolation.
- Use double quotes for strings with interpolation.
- Use 2 spaces for indentation.
- Avoid trailing whitespace.
- Use your editor to spot and trim trailing whitespace.

title: Test-Driven Development in Ruby
content:
## Rules

### Do this
  - Write tests before implementing any production code.
  - Ensure tests fail before writing implementation code.
  - Implement only enough code to make the current test pass.
  - Refactor code after tests pass, maintaining green tests.
  - Use descriptive test names and organize tests logically.

### Dont do this
  - Don’t write implementation code before writing a failing test.
  - Don’t skip writing tests for new features or bug fixes.
  - Don’t use third-party test frameworks other than RSpec unless specified.

## Examples

### Good
```rb
# spec/grid_spec.rb
describe Grid do
  it "initializes with a given size" do
    grid = Grid.new(5, 5)
    expect(grid.cells.size).to eq(5)
  end
end

# grid.rb
class Grid
  attr_reader :cells
  def initialize(rows, cols)
    @cells = Array.new(rows) { Array.new(cols, 0) }
  end
end
```

### Bad
```rb
# grid.rb
class Grid
  def initialize(rows, cols)
    @cells = Array.new(rows) { Array.new(cols, 0) }
  end
end

# spec/grid_spec.rb
# (No test written before implementation)
```

title: Ruby on Rails Performance Optimization
content:
You are an expert in Ruby on Rails performance optimization.

## View Rendering
- Use render collection: render partial: 'item', collection: @items (2x faster)
- Use collection caching: render partial: 'item', collection: @items, cached: true (1.7x faster)
- Use ViewComponent for complex/reusable view logic over partials
- Use fragment caching (Russian Doll) for expensive view portions
- Use Turbo Frames with lazy loading for below-the-fold content

## ActiveRecord Optimization
- Use eager loading: includes, preload, eager_load for N+1 prevention
- Use select to pluck only needed columns: User.select(:id, :name)
- Use pluck / pick over map(&:attr) for single column extraction
- Use find_each / find_in_batches for large dataset iteration
- Use insert_all for bulk inserts (single query, not N round-trips)
- Use exists? / any? over count > 0 for existence checks
- Add composite/partial indexes and monitor with pg_stat_statements

## Caching
- Use Russian Doll caching for nested view fragments with automatic expiry
- Use low-level caching: Rails.cache.fetch for expensive computations
- Use Solid Cache (Rails 8) for disk-based caching
- Use Redis for multi-server caching (1.5x faster than Memcached)
- Use HTTP caching: fresh_when, stale?, ETag, Last-Modified

## Background Jobs
- Use perform_all_later (Rails 7.1+) for batch enqueue (3.5x faster)
- Enqueue by IDs, not loaded AR instances: Section.limit(1000).ids
- Use Sidekiq / GoodJob / Solid Queue for job processing
- Scale workers independently from web servers

## Ruby-Level Performance
- Enable YJIT: --yjit (Ruby 3.4+) for significant speedups
- Use Array#bsearch for sorted arrays (O(log n) vs O(n))
- Avoid string allocations in hot paths
- Use frozen string literals: # frozen_string_literal: true
- Use memory-aware coding: profile with rack-mini-profiler

## Monitoring
- Use Rack Mini Profiler in development
- Use AppSignal, Scout, or New Relic for production
- Use rack-mini-profiler for real-time DB and memory profiling
- Measure: request time, DB query count, memory per request, GC stats

title: Ruby on Rails Security Best Practices
content:
You are an expert in Ruby on Rails security.

## Authentication & Authorization
- Use devise or sorcery for authentication (don't roll your own)
- Use pundit or cancancan for authorization
- Use has_secure_password for simple password auth (bcrypt)
- Use session-based auth for server-rendered apps, JWT for APIs
- Implement rate limiting on login endpoints (rack-attack)
- Use OAuth (OmniAuth) for third-party authentication

## SQL Injection Prevention
- Use ActiveRecord query methods (not raw SQL interpolation)
- If using raw SQL, always use sanitize_sql or bind variables
- Use where('name = ?', params[:name]) not where("name = '#{params[:name]}'")
- Validate and whitelist column names in dynamic order/group clauses

## XSS & CSRF
- Rails auto-escapes in ERB templates (but not .raw or .html_safe)
- Use sanitize helper for user-generated HTML content
- Use content_security_policy in config to define CSP headers
- CSRF token: Rails includes by default in forms; verify for APIs
- Use form_authenticity_token for AJAX requests
- Use Secure headers gem for comprehensive HTTP security headers

## Mass Assignment
- Use strong parameters (permit/require) in all controllers
- Never use attr_accessible or attr_protected (Rails 3 legacy)
- Be cautious with nested attributes for associations

## General Security
- Keep Rails and gems updated (bundle audit, dependabot)
- Use encrypted credentials (Rails 5.2+ credentials.yml.enc)
- Use secrets.yml or environment variables for secrets (never hardcode)
- Use rack-attack for Rack-level rate limiting
- Use rack-protection middleware for common web attacks
- Use brakeman for static security analysis in CI
- Use bundler-audit for gem vulnerability scanning

title: Rails 8 Application Architecture & Deployment
content:
You are an expert in Rails 8 application architecture and deployment.

## Rails 8 New Defaults
- Solid Cache: disk-based caching (default, replaces Redis for simple caching)
- Solid Queue: database-backed job queue (default, replaces Sidekiq for simple apps)
- Solid Cable: database-backed WebSocket adapter
- Kamal: containerized deployment tool (Capistrano for containers)
- Propshaft: modern asset pipeline (replaces Sprockets)
- Importmaps: JavaScript without bundlers (default) or jsbundling-rails

## Application Architecture
- Use modular monolith first; extract to microservices only when needed
- Use engines for bounded contexts within monolith
- Use concerns for cross-cutting model/controller logic (sparingly)
- Use service objects for complex business logic
- Use interactions or operations for multi-step workflows
- Use stimulus + turbo (Hotwire) for interactive UIs without JS frameworks
- Use Active Storage for file uploads with cloud providers
- Use Action Mailer + Active Job for email delivery

## Database & Scaling
- Use read replicas (Rails 6+ native support for switching writers/replicas)
- Use database sharding for horizontal scaling
- Use connection pooling per thread configuration
- Use pghero for PostgreSQL performance monitoring
- Use database migration best practices: zero-downtime migrations
- Avoid locking migrations (add_index concurrently, etc.)

## Deployment
- Use Kamal for containerized deployments (Docker-based)
- Use CI/CD: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or CircleCI
- Use health checks: /healthcheck endpoint for load balancer
- Use log aggregation (ELK/Loki) + structured logging
- Use APM (Scout, AppSignal, New Relic) for production monitoring
- Use error tracking (Sentry, Honeybadger)

## Testing
- Use RSpec or Minitest (Rails default)
- Use system tests (Capybara + Cuprite/Playwright) for E2E
- Use parallel testing in CI
- Use fixtures or factory_bot for test data
- Use shoulda-matchers for concise model specs
